newsitem.title: UK: EUROPEAN STOCKS, BONDS SURGE AFTER GREENSPAN.
newsitem.headline: EUROPEAN STOCKS, BONDS SURGE AFTER GREENSPAN.

text.p: European stock and bond prices rose sharply on Wednesday, following New York's surge on Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks that U.S. economic growth has moderated and inflation would be modest this year.

Analysts saw Greenspan's comments late on Tuesday as a sign that U.S. rates would remain steady in the near-term. That sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average soaring 154.93 points, or nearly two percent, to end at a record high 8,061.65 and the U.S. dollar to the highest level since August 1991.
U.S. 30-year bond prices jumped more than a point and a half, sending long-term rates down to 6.42 percent.

"Greenspan has painted a very nice picture of the U.S. economy which is very bullish for U.S. asset markets," said Jesper Dannesboe, treasury economist at ABN-Amro in London. "The strong growth and low inflation scenario is also quite bullish for the dollar."

New York's gains led German shares to open up more than 100 points and immediately race to a record high 4,418.64. But stock and bond bourse trade was suspended just after midday due to a massive systems problem.
Paris added about three percent, to score its own record high of 3,010.37 at about midmorning.
French, German and British government debt prices also rallied to new highs, lowering interest rates and lending more support to stocks.

"I have no doubt that the current stance of policy...will need to be changed at some point," Greenspan said in prepared testimony to a House Banking subcommittee on the first day of Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
"For the present, as I indicated, demand growth does appear to have moderated, but whether that moderation will be sufficient to avoid putting additional pressures on resources is an open question."

German and French shares also benefitted from the soaring dollar. The dollar hovered near 1.83 marks and hit a one-year high against the French franc. Greenspan said the U.S. current account deficit was not a problem now in light of the strong dollar.
A weaker currency makes that country's goods cheaper abroad, which is seen helping export firms.
Banking shares in Germany's DAX index and France's CAC-40 index led gains with help from merger speculation and solid earnings reports.

Monday's news that Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypobank would merge had already fired up investors, believing that a long-awaited consolidation of the fragmented banking sector might be under way.

Germany's largest bank, Deutsche Bank AG helped sentiment by reporting a 27.5 percent rise in net income. The result, above forecasts, sent its shares surging more than five percent to an all-time high.
Banque Nationale de Paris and Crdit Commercial de France in France also climbed. Credit Commercial gained more than 10 percent to notch a year high of 291.90.
London's FTSE-100 index also rose, but gains were more restrained.
NatWest markets UK strategist David McBain noted that Greenspan would address the Senate banking committee on Wednesday in the second leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony at 1400 GMT.
"We're not quite out of the woods with the second part of Greenspan's testimony this afternoon. Greenspan may try to temper the markets' reaction," he said.
Traders said the market had little reaction to a stronger-than-expected 0.6-percent rise in Britain's June retail sales. Analysts had predicted a 0.4-percent gain.
Markets were also little moved by a slightly disappointing auction of 2.0 bln stg of British government debt.
In foreign exchange markets, the dollar also continued to find support from general mark weakness and the continuing uncertainty over European economic and monetary union.

"With structural problems remaining untackled in Europe, the higher dollar will find few opponents on this side of the Atlantic," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

The only market Greenspan's comments failed to spur higher was precious metals. Gold prices slipped after Greenspan said he saw little price pressures, including those in the agricultire or industrial commodity sectors. Gold has traditionally been seen as an inflation hedge for investments.
CURRENCIES AT 1030 GMT
The dollar was at 1.8293 marks and 115.45 yen versus 1.8177 and 115.54 in late trading on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1030 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 81.1 points, or 1.67 percent, at 4,927.80.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index was up 164.57 points, or 3.89 percent, at 4,394.99.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 86.45 points, or 2.96 percent, at 3,007.58.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixeds in London at $324.35, down from $327.95 at Tuesday's close. Silver was down at $3.30.
($ = 1.804 German Marks) REUTER
